easy.text: What does a molecular formula show?

options.text: The exact number of each type of atom in one molecule
options.feedback: Correct -- a molecular formula like C₆H₁₂O₆ gives the actual atom counts in a molecule.

options.text: Only the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
options.feedback: That describes an empirical formula, not a molecular formula.

options.text: The color of the compound
options.feedback: Color isn't conveyed by a molecular formula -- it shows atom composition.

options.text: The temperature at which the compound melts
options.feedback: Melting point isn't part of a molecular formula -- it shows atom composition.

medium.text: Glucose has the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆. What is its empirical formula?

options.text: CH₂O
options.feedback: Correct -- dividing each subscript by their greatest common factor (6) gives the simplest ratio, CH₂O.

options.text: C₆H₁₂O₆
options.feedback: This is the molecular formula itself, not simplified to the smallest ratio.

options.text: C₃H₆O₃
options.feedback: This divides by 2 instead of by the full greatest common factor of 6.

options.text: CH₆O
options.feedback: This doesn't divide all three subscripts by the same consistent factor.

hard.text: Two different compounds, acetylene (C₂H₂) and benzene (C₆H₆), share the same empirical formula. What does this tell you?

options.text: They have the same simplest atom ratio, but different actual molecular structures and sizes
options.feedback: Correct -- both simplify to CH, but they are genuinely different molecules with different molecular formulas and properties.

options.text: They are actually the exact same compound
options.feedback: Despite sharing an empirical formula, they have different molecular formulas and very different properties -- they are not the same compound.

options.text: They must have the same molecular formula too
options.feedback: Their molecular formulas are different (C₂H₂ vs C₆H₆) even though the simplified empirical ratio happens to match.

options.text: One of the formulas must be incorrect
options.feedback: Both formulas can be correct -- different molecules can coincidentally share the same simplified ratio of atoms.

easy.hard: This type of formula reflects the true, complete count of atoms actually present in the molecule.
easy.medium: This formula tells you exactly how many of each atom are really in the molecule.
easy.easy: This formula shows the real, exact number of atoms in a molecule.

medium.hard: Divide every subscript in the molecular formula by their shared greatest common factor to reach the simplest ratio.
medium.medium: Divide 6, 12, and 6 all by the same number to get the simplest ratio.
medium.easy: Divide all three numbers (6, 12, 6) by 6 to simplify.

hard.hard: Multiple distinct molecular formulas can reduce to the same simplified ratio -- matching empirical formulas don't imply matching molecular structure, size, or identity.
hard.medium: Even though the simplified ratios match, the actual molecules can be totally different sizes and structures.
hard.easy: Even with the same simplified ratio, these can still be two completely different molecules.

options.text: How strongly an atom attracts shared electrons in a bond
options.feedback: Correct -- electronegativity reflects an atom's pull on bonding electrons.

options.text: How much an atom weighs
options.feedback: Atomic mass measures weight -- electronegativity is about electron attraction, a different property.

options.text: How many protons an atom has total
options.feedback: That's the atomic number -- electronegativity is a related but distinct concept about bonding behavior.

options.text: How radioactive an atom is
options.feedback: Radioactivity relates to unstable nuclei, unrelated to electronegativity.

medium.text: In a bond between two atoms with very different electronegativities, what type of bond is likely to form?

options.text: A polar covalent or ionic bond, since electrons are pulled unevenly or fully transferred
options.feedback: Correct -- a large electronegativity difference leads to uneven sharing or full electron transfer.

options.text: A perfectly nonpolar covalent bond
options.feedback: Nonpolar covalent bonds form when electronegativities are similar or equal, not very different.

options.text: No bond will form at all
options.feedback: A large electronegativity difference doesn't prevent bonding -- it actually favors ionic bond formation.

options.text: A metallic bond
options.feedback: Metallic bonding occurs between metal atoms sharing a 'sea' of electrons, which isn't primarily determined by electronegativity difference in this way.

hard.text: Water (H₂O) is a polar molecule partly because oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen. What effect does this have on the shared electrons in the O-H bonds?

options.text: The electrons spend more time near the oxygen atom, giving it a partial negative charge
options.feedback: Correct -- oxygen's stronger pull on the shared electrons creates an uneven charge distribution across the molecule.

options.text: The electrons spend equal time near both atoms
options.feedback: Equal sharing would describe a nonpolar bond, but the significant electronegativity difference here causes uneven sharing.

options.text: The electrons transfer completely to hydrogen
options.feedback: This describes ionic bonding -- but O-H bonds are still covalent (shared), just unevenly, not fully transferred to hydrogen (and to the less electronegative atom, which would be unusual).

options.text: The electronegativity difference has no effect on charge distribution
options.feedback: This difference is precisely what causes water's uneven, polar charge distribution.

easy.hard: This property reflects an atom's pulling power over electrons involved in a chemical bond.
easy.medium: This measures how much an atom 'wants' to hold onto shared electrons in a bond.
easy.easy: This measures how strongly an atom pulls on electrons it shares with another atom.

medium.hard: A large gap in electron-pulling strength between two atoms leads to either lopsided sharing or complete transfer of electrons.
medium.medium: When one atom pulls much harder on electrons than the other, the bond becomes either unevenly shared or fully transferred.
medium.easy: When one atom pulls electrons much more strongly, the bond becomes either uneven or a full transfer, not equal sharing.

hard.hard: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electron density toward itself, creating a slight negative charge there and a corresponding slight positive charge on the other atom.
hard.medium: Since oxygen pulls harder on the shared electrons, it ends up with a slightly negative charge while hydrogen ends up slightly positive.
hard.easy: Since oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer to itself, it ends up slightly negative while hydrogen ends up slightly positive.

easy.text: What type of bonding holds metal atoms together in a solid metal?

options.text: Metallic bonding
options.feedback: Correct -- metallic bonding involves a 'sea' of shared electrons among many metal atoms.

options.text: Ionic bonding
options.feedback: Ionic bonding typically occurs between a metal and a nonmetal, not between metal atoms and each other.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding
options.feedback: Hydrogen bonding is a weaker attraction relevant to molecules like water, not the bonding between metal atoms.

options.text: No bonding at all -- metal atoms simply touch
options.feedback: Metal atoms are genuinely bonded together through shared, mobile electrons, not just physically touching.

medium.text: What is the 'electron sea' model used to describe in metallic bonding?

options.text: Valence electrons that are shared freely among all the metal atoms, not tied to any one atom
options.feedback: Correct -- this pool of mobile electrons is why metals conduct electricity and heat so well.

options.text: Water molecules trapped inside a piece of metal
options.feedback: This model describes electrons, not actual water -- 'sea' is a metaphor for how freely the electrons move.

options.text: Protons floating freely between metal atoms
options.feedback: It's electrons, not protons, that move freely in this model -- protons stay fixed within their nuclei.

options.text: A literal ocean surrounding metal deposits underground
options.feedback: This is a conceptual/metaphorical model about electron behavior, not a literal body of water.

hard.text: Why are metals generally malleable (able to be hammered into sheets) without shattering?

options.text: The freely moving electrons allow metal atoms to slide past each other while the bonding holds them together
options.feedback: Correct -- unlike rigid ionic bonds, the flexible electron sea allows metal atom layers to shift without breaking the overall structure.

options.text: Metal atoms have no bonds between them at all
options.feedback: Metal atoms are definitely bonded -- it's the flexible nature of that bonding that allows shaping without breaking.

options.text: Metals are always heated before being shaped
options.feedback: While heat can help, the fundamental reason metals CAN be shaped this way relates to their bonding structure, not just temperature.

options.text: Metal atoms are unusually small compared to other atoms
options.feedback: Atomic size isn't the reason for malleability -- it's the mobile electron sea allowing atoms to shift without breaking bonds.

easy.hard: This type of bonding is unique to metals and involves electrons that aren't tied to any single atom.
easy.medium: This is the specific kind of bonding found between atoms of the same metal.
easy.easy: This is the type of bonding that holds a solid piece of metal together.

medium.hard: This model describes a shared, delocalized pool of the outermost electrons surrounding all the fixed metal atom cores.
medium.medium: This describes electrons that move freely around all the metal atoms instead of staying with just one.
medium.easy: This describes electrons that move freely around, not stuck to just one atom.

hard.hard: Because the bonding electrons aren't localized to specific atom pairs, the metal atom cores can shift position relative to each other without disrupting the overall bonding network.
hard.medium: Since the electrons aren't tied to specific atoms, the metal atoms can shift around each other without breaking apart.
hard.easy: Since the electrons can move freely, the metal atoms can slide past each other without the whole thing breaking.

easy.text: What happens to the concentration of a solution when you add more solvent (like water) without adding more solute?

options.text: The concentration decreases
options.feedback: Correct -- diluting a solution with more solvent spreads the same amount of solute over a larger volume, lowering concentration.

options.text: The concentration increases
options.feedback: Adding more solvent spreads the solute out more, which lowers concentration, not raises it.

options.text: The concentration stays exactly the same
options.feedback: Adding solvent without adding solute changes the ratio between them, which changes concentration.

options.text: The solute disappears completely
options.feedback: The solute is still present in the solution -- it's just more spread out, not gone.

medium.text: If you have 100 mL of a solution and add 100 mL more of pure water, what happens to the total volume and the amount of solute?

options.text: The total volume doubles, but the amount of solute stays the same
options.feedback: Correct -- dilution doesn't add or remove solute, it just increases the total volume it's spread through.

options.text: Both the volume and the amount of solute double
options.feedback: Only the solvent (water) was added -- no additional solute was introduced, so solute amount stays the same.

options.text: The total volume stays the same, but the solute amount doubles
options.feedback: Adding 100 mL of water definitely increases the total volume -- it doesn't add solute.

options.text: Neither the volume nor the solute amount changes
options.feedback: Adding water does increase the total volume, even though it leaves the solute amount unchanged.

hard.text: You have 50 mL of a solution with a concentration of 4 mol/L. If you dilute it to a total volume of 200 mL, what is the new concentration?

options.text: 1 mol/L
4 mol/L
options.feedback: This ignores that the volume increased, which should lower the concentration.

options.text: 16 mol/L
options.feedback: This increases rather than decreases the concentration, the opposite of what dilution does.

options.text: 0.5 mol/L
options.feedback: This doesn't match correctly applying the dilution equation with the given values.

easy.hard: Adding more of the dissolving liquid spreads the same dissolved amount over more total space.
easy.medium: The same amount of dissolved stuff is now spread across more liquid.
easy.easy: Adding more water spreads out the same amount of dissolved stuff, making it weaker.

medium.hard: Only solvent was added in this scenario -- track which quantity (volume or solute amount) that specifically affects.
medium.medium: Adding pure water increases the total liquid volume, but doesn't add any more of the dissolved substance.
medium.easy: Adding water makes the total amount of liquid bigger, but doesn't add more of the dissolved stuff.

hard.hard: Use the dilution equation (concentration × volume stays constant) to solve for the new concentration after the volume change.
hard.medium: Multiply the original concentration by the original volume, then divide by the new total volume.
hard.easy: Multiply 4 by 50, then divide that result by 200.

options.text: A mixture that looks uniform throughout, with no visibly different parts
options.feedback: Correct -- salt water is a classic example, appearing the same throughout.

options.text: A mixture with clearly visible different parts or layers
options.feedback: That describes a heterogeneous mixture, the opposite of homogeneous.

options.text: A mixture that is chemically bonded together
options.feedback: Mixtures (homogeneous or not) aren't chemically bonded -- that would make them a compound instead.

options.text: A mixture that only contains one single element
options.feedback: A homogeneous mixture can contain multiple different substances -- what matters is how uniformly they're blended.

medium.text: Which of the following is an example of a heterogeneous mixture?

options.text: A salad with visibly separate vegetables
options.feedback: Correct -- you can clearly see and separate the distinct ingredients in a salad.

options.text: Salt fully dissolved in water
options.feedback: Fully dissolved salt water looks uniform throughout, making it a homogeneous mixture.

options.text: Air (a mixture of gases)
options.feedback: Air is actually a homogeneous mixture -- the gases are evenly blended throughout.

options.text: Sugar completely dissolved in tea
options.feedback: Fully dissolved sugar in tea looks uniform, making this a homogeneous mixture.

hard.text: Muddy water, if left to sit, eventually separates into a layer of sediment at the bottom and clearer water on top. What does this indicate about muddy water as a mixture?

options.text: It is a heterogeneous mixture, since its components can settle out and aren't evenly distributed
options.feedback: Correct -- the ability of the components to separate and settle shows they weren't uniformly mixed throughout, which is the hallmark of a heterogeneous mixture.

options.text: It is a homogeneous mixture, since it initially looked uniform
options.feedback: Initial appearance can be misleading -- true homogeneous mixtures don't naturally separate into distinct layers like this.

options.text: It is a pure compound
options.feedback: A pure compound wouldn't separate into distinct visible layers -- this is a physical mixture, not a chemically bonded compound.

options.text: It is not a mixture at all
options.feedback: Muddy water is indeed a mixture of dirt particles and water -- it just happens to be heterogeneous.

easy.hard: This mixture type shows no visibly distinct regions -- everything blends together evenly.
easy.medium: Everything in this type of mixture is spread out evenly, with no visible chunks or layers.
easy.easy: This mixture looks the same all the way through, like salt water.

medium.hard: Look for the option where distinct components remain visibly separate and could be physically picked apart.
medium.medium: Look for the mixture where you can clearly see and separate its different parts.
medium.easy: Look for the mixture where you can clearly see and pick out its different parts.

hard.hard: Settling and separation over time reveals that the components were never truly, uniformly distributed at the microscopic level -- a defining trait of heterogeneous mixtures.
hard.medium: The fact that it separates on its own shows the parts weren't actually evenly blended to begin with.
hard.easy: Since it separates into layers over time, the parts weren't evenly mixed to begin with.

easy.text: What is the key difference between a chemical reaction and a nuclear reaction?

options.text: A chemical reaction involves electrons, while a nuclear reaction involves changes in the nucleus itself
options.feedback: Correct -- chemical reactions rearrange electron bonds, while nuclear reactions change protons/neutrons in the nucleus.

options.text: There is no real difference between them
options.feedback: These are fundamentally different processes occurring at very different scales within the atom.

options.text: A nuclear reaction only happens in liquids
options.feedback: Nuclear reactions aren't restricted to a particular state of matter -- the key difference is what part of the atom is involved.

options.text: A chemical reaction always releases far more energy than a nuclear reaction
options.feedback: This is backwards -- nuclear reactions typically release vastly more energy than chemical reactions.

medium.text: In a nuclear reaction, what can happen to the identity of an element?

options.text: It can change into a completely different element
options.feedback: Correct -- since nuclear reactions can change the number of protons, the element's identity itself can transform.

options.text: It always stays the exact same element, no matter what
options.feedback: Nuclear reactions can alter the number of protons, which can actually change what element it is.

options.text: It turns into a different state of matter only, not a new element
options.feedback: Nuclear reactions can fundamentally change the element itself, not just its physical state.

options.text: It becomes electrically neutral only
options.feedback: Charge neutrality isn't the defining outcome here -- the potential change in elemental identity is the key point.

hard.text: Why do nuclear reactions typically release vastly more energy than chemical reactions of similar mass?

options.text: Nuclear reactions involve the extremely strong forces holding the nucleus together, while chemical reactions only involve weaker electron interactions
options.feedback: Correct -- the forces binding protons and neutrons in the nucleus are far stronger than the electromagnetic forces involved in chemical bonding.

options.text: Nuclear reactions always involve much larger amounts of starting material
options.feedback: The huge energy difference isn't primarily about quantity of material -- it's about the fundamentally stronger forces involved in the nucleus.

options.text: Chemical reactions actually release more energy, but it's harder to measure
options.feedback: This has it backwards -- nuclear reactions genuinely release far more energy per unit mass than chemical reactions.

options.text: Nuclear reactions always happen at much colder temperatures
options.feedback: Temperature conditions aren't what explains the energy difference -- it's the type of force being tapped into (nuclear vs. electron-level).

easy.hard: One process rearranges outer particles; the other alters the dense, central core of the atom.
easy.medium: One of these processes only involves the outer electrons; the other involves the atom's core.
easy.easy: One process changes the electrons around an atom; the other changes the atom's actual core.

medium.hard: Since the core particle count (protons) can shift during this type of reaction, the fundamental identity of the atom itself can change.
medium.medium: Since this type of reaction can change the number of protons, it can turn one element into a totally different one.
medium.easy: This type of reaction can actually turn one element into a completely different element.

hard.hard: The force binding the nucleus together is fundamentally much stronger than the electromagnetic forces governing chemical bonds, so disrupting it releases proportionally far more energy.
hard.medium: The forces holding the nucleus together are much stronger than the forces involved in chemical bonds, so breaking them releases much more energy.
hard.easy: The force holding an atom's core together is much stronger than the force in chemical bonds, so nuclear reactions release way more energy.
